content: Nicotine gum is a specialized form of chewing gum designed to deliver nicotine into the body. It is primarily used as a smoking cessation aid and to help individuals quit smokeless tobacco. The nicotine is absorbed into the bloodstream through the mucosal tissues of the mouth. In the United States, nicotine gum is available over-the-counter and is typically sold in individual foil packages. It comes in various flavors, such as orange and mint, and is available in doses of 2 mg or 4 mg of nicotine per piece, which is approximately equivalent to the nicotine content of one or two cigarettes. The appropriate dosage is determined based on the user’s smoking habits. Popular brands in the UK include Nicorette and Nicotinell. Other nicotine replacement therapies include nicotine patches, lozenges, and inhalers. To use nicotine gum, the user chews it until it softens and a tingling sensation or peppery taste is noticed. At this point, the gum is placed between the cheek and gums. When the tingling subsides, the gum is chewed again and repositioned in a different area of the mouth. This process is repeated until the gum is depleted of nicotine, which typically takes about 30 minutes. The availability of nicotine gum varies globally. Initially, in the early 1990s, it was sold in the United States only by prescription. Currently, in the U.S., it is available over-the-counter at drugstores, subject to the same age restrictions as tobacco products. In some cases, the purchaser may need to consult a pharmacist, while in others, nicotine therapy products are displayed near cigarette displays. In certain locations, nicotine gum can be purchased directly off the shelf. At large retailers with self-checkout options, the gum can be purchased without human interaction, raising concerns about potential misuse by children or recreational users. In Hong Kong, stronger doses (4 mg) often require the purchaser to sign a register with identification, such as a passport or Hong Kong ID. In Paris, nicotine gum is widely available, relatively inexpensive, and sold with strict enforcement of age restrictions. However, sales to adults are less restricted, and a broad range of alternative therapies is accessible. The cost per dose in the U.S. and Hong Kong is approximately 40 cents, which can make nicotine gum more expensive than cigarettes in some regions. In countries where cigarette prices are heavily taxed, nicotine gum may be a more affordable alternative. Nicotine, the addictive component in cigarettes, also contributes to the potential for addiction to nicotine gum. Behavioral, social, and self-image factors associated with smoking further enhance its addictive nature. For example, one effective smoking cessation technique involves focusing on breathing differently when cigarette cravings arise. While studies by pharmaceutical companies suggest that switching to nicotine gum helps individuals quit both smoking and gum use, some users develop a chronic dependency on the gum. Long-term use of nicotine gum can be costly, amounting to thousands of dollars over time, despite potential health benefits (e.g., a lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s diseases). Additionally, the high cost of nicotine gum in the U.S. may drive some users to turn to hazardous alternatives, such as chewing tobacco or dip, especially if they run out of gum or cannot afford it. This issue is less prevalent in the UK, where nicotine gum is available by prescription from general practitioners, free of charge for low-income users, or at a subsidized cost through the National Health Service. New users of nicotine gum, as well as those who overuse it during periods of stress, may experience side effects such as hiccups and a sensation of throat muscle constriction. Furthermore, chewing gum is considered uncultured in many countries, which can be addressed by using nicotine pastilles. However, pastilles are not always as readily available as gum.
